content: Cefaclor is an antibiotic that is approved by the FDA for the treatment of various bacterial infections, including otitis media, lower respiratory tract infections, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, urinary tract infections, and skin and skin structure infections. It is effective against infections caused by specific susceptible microorganisms, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pyogenes. However, certain strains of Haemophilus influenzae that are β-lactamase-negative and ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR) should be considered resistant to cefaclor, even if in vitro testing suggests susceptibility. For adults, the standard dosage is 250 mg every 8 hours. In more severe infections, such as pneumonia, or when dealing with less susceptible organisms, the dose may be doubled. Cefaclor can be used in patients with impaired renal function without significant dosage adjustments, but careful monitoring is advised. In pediatric patients, the recommended dosage is 20 mg/kg/day divided into doses every 8 hours. For more serious infections, such as otitis media or infections caused by less susceptible organisms, the dosage may be increased to 40 mg/kg/day, with a maximum daily dose of 1 gram. As with adults, treatment for β-hemolytic streptococcal infections should last at least 10 days. Cefaclor is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporins. Caution is advised in patients with a history of penicillin allergy, as cross-reactivity between β-lactam antibiotics has been documented and may occur in up to 10% of such patients. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefaclor. This condition, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridium difficile, should be considered in patients presenting with diarrhea during or after antibiotic therapy. Mild cases may resolve with discontinuation of the drug, but more severe cases may require fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, and targeted antibacterial therapy against C. difficile. Adverse reactions to cefaclor include hypersensitivity reactions, such as rash, pruritus, and urticaria, which occur in approximately 1.5% of patients. Serum-sickness-like reactions, characterized by skin manifestations, arthritis, and fever, have been reported, particularly in pediatric patients and during subsequent courses of therapy. Severe hypersensitivity reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and anaphylaxis, are rare but have been documented. Gastrointestinal side effects, including diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting, occur in about 2.5% of patients. Other reported effects include eosinophilia, genital pruritus, vaginitis, and, rarely, thrombocytopenia or reversible interstitial nephritis. Cefaclor is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA, indicating that animal studies have not demonstrated harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Small amounts of cefaclor are excreted in breast milk, and caution is advised when administering the drug to nursing mothers. Cefaclor is primarily excreted by the kidneys, and elderly patients with reduced renal function may be at increased risk of toxicity. Dose adjustments may be necessary in such cases, and renal function should be monitored. In cases of overdose, symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress, and diarrhea. Treatment involves supportive care, monitoring of vital signs, and, if necessary, administration of activated charcoal to reduce drug absorption. Gastric emptying is generally not required unless a significant overdose has occurred. Cefaclor is available in capsule form, with each capsule containing either 250 mg or 500 mg of the active ingredient. It should be stored at room temperature, between 20°C and 25°C (68°F to 77°F). Patients should be counseled to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if symptoms improve, to prevent the development of antibiotic resistance.
